content: Mammary glands are specialized organs in mammals responsible for producing milk to nourish their offspring. These glands are modified sweat glands and are classified as exocrine glands. Their development and function are intricately linked to hormonal regulation and reproductive biology. Structure of Mammary Glands in Humans The mammary gland is composed of alveoli, which are small, hollow cavities lined with cuboidal epithelial cells that secrete milk. Surrounding these epithelial cells are myoepithelial cells, which have the ability to contract, similar to muscle cells. The alveoli are organized into clusters called lobules, and each lobule is connected to a lactiferous duct. These ducts converge and open at the nipple. Myoepithelial cell contraction facilitates the movement of milk from the alveoli through the ducts to the nipple, where it collects in widened areas known as sinuses. When an infant begins to suckle, the let-down reflex is triggered by hormonal signals, primarily oxytocin, which causes milk to be ejected into the infant's mouth. Milk is not actively sucked out by the infant but is instead secreted into the mouth due to this reflex. A simple mammary gland refers to all the milk-secreting tissue associated with a single lactiferous duct, while a complex mammary gland consists of multiple simple glands serving one nipple. Humans typically have two complex mammary glands, one in each breast, with each complex gland comprising 10–20 simple glands. Conditions such as polythelia (extra nipples) and polymastia (extra mammary glands) can occur. Development and Hormonal Regulation Mammary glands are present in both sexes but remain underdeveloped until puberty. In females, ovarian hormones, particularly estrogen, stimulate their development. Estrogen promotes the growth and branching of the ductal system, while testosterone inhibits this process in males. At birth, infants have lactiferous ducts but lack alveoli. During puberty, ovarian estrogens induce further branching and differentiation of the ducts into spherical cell clusters that will later form alveoli. True secretory alveoli develop only during pregnancy, driven by elevated levels of estrogen and progesterone. These hormones stimulate further ductal branching, differentiation, and an increase in adipose tissue and blood supply. Late in pregnancy and shortly after birth, colostrum—a nutrient-rich, antibody-containing fluid—is secreted. Lactation, or true milk secretion, begins a few days postpartum as circulating progesterone levels decrease and prolactin levels rise. The act of suckling by the infant stimulates the release of oxytocin, which causes the myoepithelial cells to contract and expel milk. Breast Cancer The cells of the mammary glands are highly responsive to hormonal signals, which can stimulate their growth and proliferation. However, if this growth becomes dysregulated, it can lead to cancer. Nearly all cases of breast cancer originate in the lobules or ducts of the mammary glands. Mammary Glands in Other Mammals The number and positioning of mammary glands vary widely among mammals. These glands and their associated nipples are located along two milk lines, which run parallel along the ventral side of the body. Most mammals develop mammary glands in pairs, with the number of glands roughly corresponding to the typical litter size. For example, primates generally have two nipples, while pigs have up to 16. The Virginia opossum is unique in having 13 nipples, an odd number. Male mammals usually have rudimentary mammary glands and nipples, though exceptions exist, such as male mice and horses, which lack nipples entirely. Interestingly, the male Dyak fruit bat is capable of lactation. Transgenic Applications Mammary glands are highly efficient protein production systems. This has led to the development of transgenic animals, such as goats and cows, engineered to produce pharmaceutical proteins in their milk. These proteins, including complex glycoproteins like monoclonal antibodies and antithrombin, are challenging to produce in bacterial systems and are more cost-effective to obtain from live mammals than from mammalian cell cultures. Evolution of Mammary Glands Mammary glands are believed to have evolved from modified sweat glands, specifically apocrine sweat glands. The exact evolutionary pathway remains unclear due to the poor fossilization of soft tissues. One hypothesis suggests that mammary glands originated from glands that early mammals used to keep their eggs moist.
